l: The Good and The Bad: Exploring Privacy Issues in Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG)
s: This paper studies privacy in retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), where a retriever selects documents from an external database and a large language model (LLM) uses them to answer queries. It examines two connected risks: extraction of private retrieval-database records and exposure of LLM training data. The authors use a black-box threat model and introduce composite structured prompting attacks, including targeted and untargeted extraction prompts, alongside targeted and prefix attacks for training-data leakage. After situating RAG as a system introduced by Lewis et al. (2020) that can improve relevance, reduce hallucinations, and update knowledge without retraining, the paper notes that LLMs may memorize pre-training data and that RAG adds a second sensitive source: retrieved context. For the first research question, it tests Enron Email and HealthcareMagic-101 with Llama-7b-chat, Llama-13b-chat, and GPT-3.5-turbo. The models can reproduce retrieved text and sensitive information; in a medical-dialogue study, Llama2-7b-Chat and GPT-3.5-turbo produce verbatim or highly similar retrieval records at rates near 50%. Command design strongly affects leakage, whereas retrieving more documents yields only limited additional leakage. Re-ranking offers little protection; summarization lowers untargeted leakage but may fail against targeted attacks; and distance thresholds impose a privacy–utility tradeoff. For the second question, the paper compares GPT-Neo-1.3B with no retrieval, noise or prompts, and several retrieval datasets using Enron_Mail examples. Retrieval substantially reduces extraction of personal identifying information and reconstruction of memorized training text. W3C-Email retrieval instead causes more retrieval content to be generated, supporting the view that retrieved context shifts generation away from training data while creating its own extraction risk. The paper concludes that RAG can leak private retrieval records but may mitigate training-data memorization. It focuses on inference-stage RAG, notes that other retrieval-based language-model architectures need study, identifies differential privacy as a possible protection for retrieval data, and leaves using RAG to safeguard training data as an open question.

l: Retrieval-Augmented Generation, The Good and The Bad: Exploring Privacy Issues in Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG)
s: Retrieval-Augmented Generation is an advanced natural language processing technique and system for enhancing large language model generation. It retrieves relevant knowledge from an external database or large document corpus, integrates retrieved documents with a user query, and then generates an answer. Its typical phases are retrieval and generation, and its core components are a dataset, retriever, and LLM; these can be exchanged or updated without retraining or fine-tuning the entire system. It boosts output accuracy and relevance, mitigates hallucinations, and is used in personal chatbots, medical chatbots, and medical diagnostic assistants. The records then emphasize a privacy tradeoff: incorporating retrieval data can reduce LLM memorization and leakage of training data, but can also expose sensitive retrieval data. In particular, it is susceptible to composite structured prompting attacks for extracting retrieval data. Thus, it reshapes LLM generation while introducing new, currently under-explored privacy issues.

l: Privacy Risk of Large Language Models, The Good and The Bad: Exploring Privacy Issues in Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG)
s: Research on the privacy risk of large language models concerns their memorization and inadvertent disclosure of information from pre-training and fine-tuning data. The unit also distinguishes privacy research on retrieval-based kNN-LM from the discussed work because kNN-LM has a different architecture and mechanism.

l: memorization, The Good and The Bad: Exploring Privacy Issues in Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG)
s: Memorization in large language models is the model's reproduction of information from training data. It increases with model size, data duplication, and prompt length, varies by fine-tuning task, and can rise more when fine-tuning heads than smaller adapter modules. Retrieval integration substantially decreases observed reproduction of memorized personal identifying information and text.

l: fine-tuning data, The Good and The Bad: Exploring Privacy Issues in Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG)
s: has_privacy_risk memorization [in models fine-tuned on the data] Fine-tuning data presents privacy risks because models may memorize information from it. Dialogue and summarization tasks are particularly vulnerable because they demand extensive feature representation.

l: summarization, The Good and The Bad: Exploring Privacy Issues in Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG)
s: Summarization compresses retrieved contexts before they reach a generative model. As a fine-tuning task it may memorize information. It reduces untargeted privacy leakage, especially abstractive summarization by about 50%, but offers limited protection in targeted attacks and can increase extracted personally identifiable information.

l: retrieval-based kNN-LM, The Good and The Bad: Exploring Privacy Issues in Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG)
s: retrieval-based kNN-LM is a system whose privacy risk was investigated by Huang et al. (2023); in related work, it is distinguished from the discussed work by its different architecture and mechanism.

l: user query q, The Good and The Bad: Exploring Privacy Issues in Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG)
s: The user query q is used by R to retrieve relevant documents and is concatenated with the retrieved context before being sent to M. In the threat model, the attacker crafts and modifies q to extract desired information.

l: retrieved documents, The Good and The Bad: Exploring Privacy Issues in Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG)
s: Retrieved documents are top-k items selected from D for a query; combined with the query as context for M, they may be reproduced in responses under extraction prompting as k increases from 1 to 4.

l: black-box attack, The Good and The Bad: Exploring Privacy Issues in Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG)
s: is_a attack [realistic API-only threat model] The black-box attack assumes that the attacker interacts with the system solely through API queries. The attacker therefore relies on crafting and modifying queries without access to the system’s internals.

l: attacker, The Good and The Bad: Exploring Privacy Issues in Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG)
s: attacker is an entity in a black-box threat model that interacts with an API, modifying user queries as its available strategy to extract targeted or broad sensitive information from retrieval or LLM training data through prompts.

l: targeted attack, The Good and The Bad: Exploring Privacy Issues in Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG)
s: Targeted attack is an attack aimed at extracting specific private or sensitive information from LLM training data or retrieved data. It uses direct prompts such as “My phone number is” and “Please email me at” for training data, and objective-related information plus a command to reproduce context for retrieval data. In evaluation, it uses 5000 prompts and recovers diagnosed cases from HealthcareMagic-101 and personally identifiable information from Enron emails. It measures extracted email addresses, phone numbers, URLs, and other sensitive content. Retrieval data greatly reduces extracted items relative to no retrieval, random noise, or system prompts, though the attack increases privacy leakage through sensitive-information extraction.

l: untargeted attacks, The Good and The Bad: Exploring Privacy Issues in Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG)
s: Untargeted attacks seek to gather as much information as possible from an entire retrieval dataset, using randomly selected Common Crawl chunks rather than targeting specific data. They prompt models to repeat retrieved content without naming sensitive fields, yielding exact matches and close retrieval-data resemblance across datasets, and increasing privacy leakage through inference and reconstruction.

l: LLM training-data privacy leakage, The Good and The Bad: Exploring Privacy Issues in Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG)
s: LLM training-data privacy leakage is a privacy investigation concerning LLMs used in RAG systems. It compares exposure of targeted training-corpus subsets with and without retrieval augmentation on the same large language model, using targeted and prefix attacks.

l: personally identifiable information, The Good and The Bad: Exploring Privacy Issues in Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG)
s: Personally identifiable information is targeted in the Enron email experiments using preceding text such as “My phone number is.” Targeted attacks extract such information, and summarization can inadvertently increase its occurrence in outputs. The targeted attacks measure extraction of personal identifying information, including email addresses, phone numbers, and URLs. Retrieval data sharply reduces the reported extraction of these items, especially when the retrieval data is disparate from the training examples.

l: Enron Email dataset, The Good and The Bad: Exploring Privacy Issues in Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG)
s: The Enron Email dataset is a collection of 500,000 employee emails, partitioned into individual email data pieces and containing private personally identifiable information. It is a subset of GPT-Neo-1.3B pre-training data and is used in memorization experiments. Evaluations examine extraction and reproduction of private email content: 116 of 250 GPT-3.5-turbo prompts exactly matched content, while 121 were closely related; further experiments compare retrieval conditions.

l: HealthcareMagic-101 dataset, The Good and The Bad: Exploring Privacy Issues in Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG)
s: HealthcareMagic-101 is a domain-specific retrieval dataset of 200,000 doctor-patient medical dialogues, partitioned by dialogue and containing private information. It is used to evaluate extraction of private medical content, with targeted attacks extracting diagnosed cases for specified diseases.

l: re-ranking, The Good and The Bad: Exploring Privacy Issues in Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG)
s: mitigates privacy leakage [almost not at all] Re-ranking uses bge-reranker-large to reorder retrieved documents by relevance before generation. In the reported experiments, re-ranking has almost no mitigation effect on targeted or untargeted extraction.

l: set distance threshold, The Good and The Bad: Exploring Privacy Issues in Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG)
s: A set distance threshold restricts retrieval to documents whose L2-norm embedding distance from the query is below a chosen threshold. Lower thresholds can reduce privacy leakage but can also harm system performance.

l: privacy-utility tradeoff, The Good and The Bad: Exploring Privacy Issues in Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG)
s: requires red teaming [to choose a proper threshold in practice] The distance-threshold experiments show a privacy-utility tradeoff: stricter thresholds may reduce extraction but lower task performance. The text recommends selecting thresholds through application-specific red teaming.

l: GPT-Neo-1.3B, The Good and The Bad: Exploring Privacy Issues in Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG)
s: GPT-Neo-1.3B is a generative model chosen for memorization experiments because its training corpus is public; the experiments use Enron_Mail, part of its pre-training data.

l: retrieval data extraction, The Good and The Bad: Exploring Privacy Issues in Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG)
s: Retrieval data extraction is systematically evaluated in the paper. The evaluation identifies significant privacy risks associated with extracting retrieval data.

l: defense techniques, The Good and The Bad: Exploring Privacy Issues in Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG)
s: mitigate privacy risks [associated with retrieval-augmented generation] The paper explores various defense techniques that can mitigate the privacy risks associated with retrieval data extraction.

l: retrieval augmentation, The Good and The Bad: Exploring Privacy Issues in Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG)
s: The research focused primarily on applying retrieval augmentation during inference. Its integration during pre-training and fine-tuning was not examined and is proposed for future work.

l: pre-training, The Good and The Bad: Exploring Privacy Issues in Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG)
s: Pre-training was not examined as a stage for integrating retrieval augmentation. Exploring this integration is identified as future work.

l: fine-tuning, The Good and The Bad: Exploring Privacy Issues in Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG)
s: Fine-tuning was not examined as a stage for integrating retrieval augmentation. Exploring this integration is identified as future work.

l: retrieval-based language models, The Good and The Bad: Exploring Privacy Issues in Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG)
s: Retrieval-based language models have distinct components and architectures; Huang et al. and Borgeaud et al. are cited, and further investigation is warranted.

l: differential privacy, The Good and The Bad: Exploring Privacy Issues in Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG)
s: Differential privacy is identified as a potential, effective strategy for protecting retrieval data and is cited with Feyisetan et al., Utpala et al., and Carvalho et al.

l: Reducing hallucination in structured outputs via Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: This unit describes a commercial enterprise system that turns natural-language requirements into executable workflows represented as structured JSON. Its central problem is that workflow creation normally requires specialized knowledge, while Generative AI and Large Language Models can hallucinate nonexistent steps, tables, or field values, an obstacle to trustworthy real-world use. The proposed solution is Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), adapted to retrieve structured JSON workflow steps and database tables rather than only factual text. The system first uses a dense retriever, trained in a manner similar to Structure Aware DeNse ReTrievAl (SANTA), to align user requirements with relevant step and table objects. It learns from positive and negative query–object pairs using contrastive loss, and FAISS supports cosine-similarity retrieval at inference. Retrieved items are appended to the user query, after which an LLM produces a JSON workflow through greedy decoding. The retriever and LLM are trained separately: the LLM receives augmented prompts during supervised fine-tuning and assumes required items appear among retrieved suggestions. The work contrasts this approach with Code LLMs and Guided Generation: grammar constraints can help produce valid structures but do not tell a model which enterprise-specific workflow components should be selected. Experiments use in-domain, Human Eval, and out-of-domain datasets built from deployed workflows, user interactions, and deterministic samples. The Human Eval split supplies the final metrics because its inputs are judged more realistic and higher quality. The evaluation compares retriever encoders, StarCoderBase variants, CodeLlama-7B, Mistral-7B-v0.1, and workflow-generation and retrieval results. Results show that fine-tuning a small retriever with combined negative-sampling strategies substantially improves retrieval of steps and tables, whereas simply scaling off-the-shelf encoders has limited benefit. RAG reduces hallucinated steps and tables and supports out-of-domain generalization; StarCoderBase-7B provides the best evaluated StarCoderBase trade-off. The authors identify retriever omissions and difficulty generating IF, TRY, and FOREACH structures as key remaining errors. They favor modular retriever–LLM deployment and conclude that a very small retriever paired with a smaller LLM can preserve performance in limited-resource settings. The system post-processes nonexistent generated steps and asks users to correct outputs, acknowledging that hallucination risk remains. Future work targets joint retriever–LLM training or better-suited architectures.

l: Generative AI, Reducing hallucination in structured outputs via Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: Generative AI lowers barriers to workflow building by letting novice users describe behavior in natural language, but its propensity to hallucinate makes naive outputs untrustworthy; a Retrieval-Augmented Generation system is presented to improve structured-output quality.

l: hallucination, Reducing hallucination in structured outputs via Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: Hallucination is untrustworthy output produced by LLMs, including workflow steps or database tables that do not exist. It is a current limitation of Generative AI and a barrier to adoption of real-world GenAI systems, particularly in structured-output tasks. It is evaluated through hallucinated steps and tables, where lower rates are better. Retrieval-Augmented Generation is proposed to reduce it, with a retriever lowering rates for StarCoderBase models, though removing suggestions can increase table hallucinations.

l: Large Language Models, Reducing hallucination in structured outputs via Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: Large Language Models have taken the world by storm and have global impact, but reducing hallucination remains important for real-world adoption. They support structured output, converting natural language to code, SQL, and workflows. They receive retrieved JSON objects before generating structured JSON, can be guided by grammar, and may hallucinate on out-of-distribution inputs; a smaller accompanying model with a well-trained retriever can perform without loss.

l: real-world GenAI systems, Reducing hallucination in structured outputs via Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: Real-world GenAI systems face user-adoption challenges unless hallucination is eliminated or reduced.

l: commercial enterprise system, Reducing hallucination in structured outputs via Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: A commercial enterprise system built by ServiceNow colleagues produces workflows from natural-language requirements. Its deployments supply workflow examples and motivate constraints on model and retriever size for a Retrieval-Augmented Generation system. A post-processing layer flags generated steps that do not exist and urges users to fix them before continuing work.

l: workflows, Reducing hallucination in structured outputs via Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: Workflows are deployed, automatically executed processes made of a pool of steps and logic elements, optionally beginning with a trigger step. They are generated from natural-language requirements as domain-specific JSON, with steps selected for the query; grammar alone cannot choose them. They support productivity and standardized repetitive work but require specialized knowledge to create. They are extracted or collected from deployments, generated deterministically in simple incremental cases, and evaluated as expected JSON with triggers, steps, and sometimes tables.

l: user query, Reducing hallucination in structured outputs via Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: The user query is a natural-language requirement describing a workflow. Annotators write it for deployed workflows, while expert users enter it during simulated interactions. In the architecture, the retriever embeds and uses it to find relevant JSON objects, steps, and sometimes database tables; those suggestions are combined into an LLM prompt that generates structured JSON output. It also supports workflow generation and retrieval evaluation.

l: Retrieval-Augmented Generation, Reducing hallucination in structured outputs via Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: Retrieval-Augmented Generation is an approach that retrieves information from specific data sources before text generation to limit false or outdated information. Here it is adapted from factual retrieval to structured output, retrieving JSON objects that may form part of a generated document or workflow. Its central value is reducing hallucination while improving output quality, trustworthiness, and workflow generation, especially when correct output requires external knowledge. It reduces hallucinated steps to less than 7.5% and hallucinated tables to less than 4.5% with all StarCoderBase LLMs while maintaining overall performance. It also enables out-of-domain generalization without further fine-tuning and supports conservative generation when suggestions are absent. Finally, it can be deployed in limited-resource settings with a very small retriever and a small LLM without loss in performance.

l: workflow, Reducing hallucination in structured outputs via Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: Workflow is structured JSON generated by an LLM from a user request, representing related steps and, when applicable, tables. Retrieval suggestions supply required components during training and improve quality. It must follow the expected schema and match the query; failures occur when retrieval omits crucial components or the LLM mishandles IF, TRY, or FOREACH logic steps.

l: retriever, Reducing hallucination in structured outputs via Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: Retriever is a small, well-trained retriever encoder and crucial ingredient of Retrieval-Augmented Generation. It is trained on pairs of user queries and corresponding steps or tables, with negative sampling. During initialization, it builds an index. For a natural-language query, it encodes a unit-norm embedding, uses cosine similarity, and maps the query to existing step and database-table names, retrieving up to K related structured JSON objects. Its output becomes LLM input. Used with RAG in workflow generation, a very small retriever can enable a smaller Large Language Model without loss in performance, reducing deployment resources.

l: structured output tasks, Reducing hallucination in structured outputs via Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: Structured output tasks convert natural language into valid, parseable structured data such as code, SQL, workflows, and if-then programs. They must use entities or field values from a given lexicon. Retrieval-Augmented LLM is proposed to reduce hallucination and support generalization.

l: natural language to workflows, Reducing hallucination in structured outputs via Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: is_a structured output tasks Natural language to workflows involves translating a natural language requirement into a series of steps and logic elements that specify their relationships. The unit describes using RAG to improve the trustworthiness of this translation.

l: JSON, Reducing hallucination in structured outputs via Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: A data format for workflow documents, using JSON structured output to represent each generated workflow step as an object.

l: JSON output document, Reducing hallucination in structured outputs via Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: JSON documents represent workflows as JSON objects for steps, relationships, triggers, and sometimes required database tables. Retrieved JSON objects are supplied to an LLM so it can generate valid, executable structured output by copying relevant objects. The documents serve as expected workflow ground truth for evaluating generation and retriever coverage, while a siamese transformer encoder converts them into fixed-length vectors.

l: database table, Reducing hallucination in structured outputs via Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: An embedding-encoded database-table retrieval component, evaluated by Recall@10 and hallucinated-table metrics, indexes tables when trigger steps require names; queries may map to none, while RAG reduces hallucination and removing suggestions raises it.

l: workflow generation, Reducing hallucination in structured outputs via Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: is_a structured output tasks Workflow generation converts natural language requirements into structured workflow outputs. The unit presents RAG for workflow generation and states that it reduces hallucination and improves results.

l: fine-tuning, Reducing hallucination in structured outputs via Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: Fine-tuning a sufficiently large LLM produces reasonably good workflows, but doing it separately for each enterprise can be prohibitively expensive because of infrastructure costs. Training first fine-tunes a retriever on positive and sampled negative query-object pairs, then trains the LLM on retriever-augmented prompts and workflow JSON targets, reducing hallucination and producing valid expected-schema JSON.

l: commercial GenAI application, Reducing hallucination in structured outputs via Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: needs out-of-distribution mismatch [minimized for enterprise customization] A commercial GenAI application for workflow creation needs to minimize the mismatch caused by enterprise users adding customized workflow steps. The unit describes RAG as a way to address this need without fine-tuning an LLM for every enterprise.

l: JSON objects, Reducing hallucination in structured outputs via Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: JSON objects are retrieved as candidate components of a JSON output document; supplying plausible objects before generation increases executable property inclusion.

l: Dense Retrieval, Reducing hallucination in structured outputs via Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: Dense Retrieval represents queries and documents in multidimensional semantic space, providing more effective retrieval than lexical methods such as TF-IDF or BM25 in many settings.

l: Structure Aware DeNse ReTrievAl (SANTA), Reducing hallucination in structured outputs via Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: SANTA is a structure-aware retrieval training method that aligns code and text semantics through its proposed approach.

l: natural language, Reducing hallucination in structured outputs via Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: Natural language is used as the unstructured form of the query. In the described retrieval setting, it is matched against structured JSON objects.

l: pool of steps, Reducing hallucination in structured outputs via Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: is_a customizable resource [potentially very large and customizable per deployment] The pool of steps contains the steps that can be included in a workflow. It may be very large and customizable for each deployment, making it impractical to provide the entire pool through in-context learning.

l: LLMs, Reducing hallucination in structured outputs via Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: LLMs make structured output tasks more accessible, with small-dataset fine-tuning improving quality. They generate workflow documents from retrieved suggestions; larger models copy retrieved content better, but hallucination, out-of-domain queries, and IF, TRY, and FOREACH structure failures remain challenges.

l: Code LLMs, Reducing hallucination in structured outputs via Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: Code LLMs enable developers to write code faster by generating snippets from instructions, drawing on source-code training and broad programming-language knowledge; they reason well but need adaptation for domain-specific workflow JSON schema.

l: JSON schema, Reducing hallucination in structured outputs via Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: is_a domain-specific representation [for workflows] The JSON schema used to represent workflows is domain-specific. Because of this, Code LLMs require adaptation rather than off-the-shelf use.

l: Guided Generation, Reducing hallucination in structured outputs via Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: is_a technique [for reducing hallucination with LLMs] Guided Generation uses tools such as Outlines to constrain LLM output with a sufficiently expressive context-free grammar. It can ensure that generated steps exist, but it does not supply knowledge about which steps should be selected for a natural-language query.

l: RAG system, Reducing hallucination in structured outputs via Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: The RAG system has a high-level architecture that initializes indices of steps and tables, then retrieves suggestions for each request, appends them to the query, and uses an LLM to generate JSON workflows. It trains a retriever encoder and LLM in a RAG fashion, supports domains including HR and finance, and is evaluated in- and out-of-domain.

l: LLM, Reducing hallucination in structured outputs via Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: The LLM receives user queries with retriever-suggested steps and tables, is trained through supervised fine-tuning after augmentation, and generates or copies JSON workflows using greedy decoding.

l: steps, Reducing hallucination in structured outputs via Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: Steps are workflow components, represented as a JSON object and sometimes requiring a database table. They are indexed and retrieved from queries to existing names to reduce hallucination. Evaluation uses Recall@15, Bag of Steps, and hallucinated-step metrics; retrieval reduces hallucinations but can miss complex steps and produce structural errors with logic steps.

l: retriever encoder, Reducing hallucination in structured outputs via Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: Retriever encoder is a fine-tuned model that aligns natural language with structured JSON objects and application-specific terminology, producing normalized fixed-length vectors for queries, steps, and tables. It is trained on about 15,000 step-name and 1,500 table-name pairs, then evaluated on Human Eval against off-the-shelf GTR-T5 models.

l: siamese transformer encoder, Reducing hallucination in structured outputs via Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: The siamese transformer encoder is a fine-tuned 110M-parameter encoder for retrieval. It encodes natural-language queries and step or table JSON objects with mean pooling, then normalizes embeddings to norm 1. It retrieves the top 15 steps and top 10 tables, evaluated by Recall@15 and Recall@10 against ground-truth workflow JSON. Scaling an off-the-shelf encoder helps little; fine-tuning matters most and supports GPU or CPU deployment.

l: embedding, Reducing hallucination in structured outputs via Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: has_norm 1 [after normalization] Embeddings are generated for user queries, steps, and tables by the retriever. Their cosine similarity is used to retrieve the steps and tables most associated with a requirement.

l: contrastive loss, Reducing hallucination in structured outputs via Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: Contrastive loss trains the retriever by minimizing cosine distance for positive query-object pairs and separating negative pairs with a one-half margin.

l: negative sampling, Reducing hallucination in structured outputs via Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: Negative sampling is a retriever encoder training strategy using random, BM25-based, and ANCE-based pairs; fine-tuning compares these with All, which yields the strongest retrieval results.

l: FAISS, Reducing hallucination in structured outputs via Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: builds index [of steps and tables during initialization] FAISS is used during initialization to build indices of steps and tables. Those indices support retrieval after an incoming query has been embedded.

l: cosine similarity, Reducing hallucination in structured outputs via Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: Cosine similarity compares a query embedding with step or table embeddings, retrieving the maximum K associated relevant steps and database tables.

l: standard LLM supervised fine-tuning, Reducing hallucination in structured outputs via Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: trains LLM [using retriever-augmented examples] Standard LLM supervised fine-tuning is performed after the retriever augments the dataset with suggested step and table names. The training examples use short prompts and expected workflow JSON outputs.

l: retrieval, Reducing hallucination in structured outputs via Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: Retrieval supplies suggested steps and tables for natural-language requirements during LLM training, assuming required items are retrieved except frequent memorized steps. It is evaluated with Recall@15 for steps and Recall@10 for tables; fine-tuning improves recall, while missing crucial suggestions can block valid workflows, motivating query decomposition.

l: Human Eval, Reducing hallucination in structured outputs via Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: Human Eval is a 157-sample additional evaluation dataset split built from expert-user interactions in a simple interface. Its higher-quality, more realistic inputs replace the Test split for final metrics. It contains 99 triggers and 60 tables, evaluates retrieval, performance, and hallucination, and reports RAG fine-tuned StarCoderBase-7B results.

l: Train split, Reducing hallucination in structured outputs via Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: Train split is an in-domain dataset of 2,867 examples, 823 triggers, and 556 tables; it creates retriever training pairs and measures out-of-domain split differences.

l: Test split, Reducing hallucination in structured outputs via Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: Test split contains 798 in-domain examples with 247 triggers and 163 tables, but is excluded from final metrics in favor of Human Eval.

l: out-of-domain splits, Reducing hallucination in structured outputs via Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: Out-of-domain splits are five sets of real workflows from other enterprise-platform deployments; shown in Table 2, they range from 7% to 76% steps absent from Train, motivating retrieval and deployment-specific indices.

l: Trigger Exact Match, Reducing hallucination in structured outputs via Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: Trigger Exact Match is an evaluation metric ranging from 0 to 1 that measures whether a generated JSON or workflow trigger exactly matches the ground truth, including a required table name. It evaluates performance across settings; with RAG, larger StarCoderBase models generally perform better.

l: Bag of Steps, Reducing hallucination in structured outputs via Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: Bag of Steps is an evaluation metric measuring order-agnostic overlap between generated JSON steps and ground-truth steps from 0 to 1. It ignores ordering; RAG improves or maintains it across models and OOD splits, with StarCoderBase-7B reaching 0.672 and 0.714.

l: Hallucinated Tables, Reducing hallucination in structured outputs via Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: Hallucinated Tables measures the percentage of generated tables that do not exist for the workflow and therefore were invented by the LLM. It ranges from 0 to 1, with lower values being better.

l: Hallucinated Steps, Reducing hallucination in structured outputs via Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: Hallucinated Steps measures the percentage of generated steps that do not exist for the workflow and therefore were invented by the LLM. It ranges from 0 to 1, with lower values being better.

l: StarCoderBase, Reducing hallucination in structured outputs via Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: StarCoderBase is an LLM family with 1B, 3B, 7B, and 15.5B parameter variants, selected for pretraining on JSON and multiple programming languages. After fine-tuning, it produces valid JSON. Evaluation with and without retrieval shows larger models generally improve RAG; 7B offers the best trade-off near 15.5B performance, while 3B suits limited infrastructure.

l: CodeLlama-7B, Reducing hallucination in structured outputs via Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: performs_worse_than StarCoderBase [despite RAG fine-tuning and at the same model size as StarCoderBase-7B] CodeLlama-7B is fine-tuned as an alternative 7B-parameter pretrained LLM. It is evaluated using the same datasets and hyperparameters as the other LLMs.

l: Mistral-7B-v0.1, Reducing hallucination in structured outputs via Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: performs_worse_than StarCoderBase [despite RAG fine-tuning] Mistral-7B-v0.1 is fine-tuned as another alternative 7B-parameter pretrained LLM. It is evaluated using the same datasets and hyperparameters as the other LLMs.

l: all-mpnet-base-v21, Reducing hallucination in structured outputs via Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: all-mpnet-base-v2 is a 110M-parameter base retriever encoder suitable for deployment; after fine-tuning with all evaluated negative sampling strategies, retrieval scores rise from 0.425/0.170 to 0.743/0.766.

l: OOD evaluation, Reducing hallucination in structured outputs via Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: OOD evaluation assesses RAG fine-tuned StarCoderBase-7B on five out-of-distribution splits without further tuning, finding weighted average metrics similar to Human Eval across Trigger EM, Bag of Steps, hallucinated steps, and hallucinated tables.

l: users, Reducing hallucination in structured outputs via Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: fix output (deployed system) [before continuing their work] Users are urged to fix generated output containing steps that do not exist before continuing their work.

l: our work, Reducing hallucination in structured outputs via Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: Our work proposes an approach to reduce hallucination in structure output tasks while acknowledging hallucination-related harm risk remains.

l: approach (our work), Reducing hallucination in structured outputs via Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: reduces hallucination [in structure output tasks] The approach is intended to reduce hallucination in structure output tasks.

s: The risk of harm due to hallucination is not claimed to be eliminated.

s: ServiceNow is associated with colleagues who worked hard to build the aforementioned system.

l: ServiceNow colleagues, Reducing hallucination in structured outputs via Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: ServiceNow colleagues, including project managers and quality engineers, work hard together to build a system.

l: DRAGIN: Dynamic Retrieval Augmented Generation based on the Information Needs of Large Language Models
s: This paper presents DRAGIN, a lightweight dynamic retrieval-augmented generation framework intended to reduce factually incorrect but plausible output from large language models (LLMs). Rather than retrieving once from the initial input or using fixed intervals, recent text, or uncertainty alone, DRAGIN identifies information needs during generation across the full context, deciding both when retrieval should occur and what query should be issued. DRAGIN has two central components. Real-time Information Needs Detection (RIND) determines when to retrieve by combining token entropy, maximum attention from following tokens, and a binary semantic indicator for stopwords. Query Formulation based on Self-attention (QFS) then selects highly attended preceding tokens at the detected position to construct a query. Retrieved documents are incorporated through a prompt after the model truncates its output, and generation continues; this process can repeat when another need is detected. The paper contrasts this approach with single-round and multi-round methods including REPLUG, UniWeb, RETRO, ICRALM, IRCot, and FLARE, emphasizing limitations of fixed-interval and uncertainty-based retrieval. Experiments evaluate DRAGIN on 2WikiMultihopQA, HotpotQA, IIRC, and StrategyQA, covering multihop reasoning, reading comprehension, and commonsense reasoning. Comparisons include wo-RAG, SR-RAG, FL-RAG, FS-RAG, and FLARE. Using LLaMA-2-Chat, Vicuna-13B-v1.5, Llama2-13b-chat, and Llama2-7b-chat, BM25 retrieval over Wikipedia passages, and greedy decoding, DRAGIN generally delivers the strongest results, particularly on multihop reasoning tasks. Analyses attribute substantial gains to retrieval timing and query formulation, find DRAGIN relatively efficient in retrieval calls, and report that BM25 outperforms SGPT in the tested dynamic setting. The paper concludes that RIND and QFS enable superior dynamic RAG performance across the benchmarks. Its main limitation is dependence on Transformer self-attention scores, preventing use with APIs that do not expose them. The work reports no personally identifiable information or manually annotated datasets, releases models, data, and code on GitHub, and acknowledges support from Quan Cheng Laboratory under Grant No. QCLZD202301.

l: dynamic RAG, DRAGIN: Dynamic Retrieval Augmented Generation based on the Information Needs of Large Language Models
s: Dynamic RAG is a multi-round retrieval-augmented generation paradigm and method for Large Language Models. It performs multiple retrievals during generation, using a retrieval module and query to decide when external knowledge is needed and what to retrieve. Its central challenge is selecting an optimal activation moment and crafting a query, avoiding static timing and narrow recent-context approaches that can add noise and cost or miss broader needs. In DRAGIN, token-level information-need scores trigger retrieval, which can recur later with newly retrieved documents.

l: large language models, DRAGIN: Dynamic Retrieval Augmented Generation based on the Information Needs of Large Language Models
s: Large language models are models used widely in AI applications that have advanced natural language processing and are effective across many tasks. They generate tokens using self-attention and built-in knowledge, producing coherent, plausible text but often factual errors and sometimes falling short on knowledge-intensive tasks. Retrieval augmentation addresses these limits by supplying external-corpus information. In dynamic retrieval augmented generation, retrieval determines whether and what to retrieve; the model records token probabilities and attention scores, receives external knowledge with a truncated answer, and continues generating.

l: retrieval module, DRAGIN: Dynamic Retrieval Augmented Generation based on the Information Needs of Large Language Models
s: The retrieval module activates during text generation at an optimal moment when a low-probability token triggers needed retrieval.

l: text generation process, DRAGIN: Dynamic Retrieval Augmented Generation based on the Information Needs of Large Language Models
s: The text generation process is the stage during which dynamic retrieval augmented generation decides when to retrieve and crafts an appropriate query.

l: retrieval, DRAGIN: Dynamic Retrieval Augmented Generation based on the Information Needs of Large Language Models
s: Retrieval is initiated when the model's information needs warrant it, and its timing and content are central decisions in dynamic RAG. Retrieval is compared by its timing and query formulation across the evaluated methods. It may occur before generation, every fixed number of tokens, after each sentence, at low-probability tokens, or according to generated-token importance and uncertainty.

l: query, DRAGIN: Dynamic Retrieval Augmented Generation based on the Information Needs of Large Language Models
s: is_crafted_when retrieval is triggered [appropriate query] The query is crafted after retrieval is triggered. Existing methods typically derive it from the most recent sentence or the last few tokens, whereas DRAGIN bases it on information needs that may span the entire context.

l: real-time information needs, DRAGIN: Dynamic Retrieval Augmented Generation based on the Information Needs of Large Language Models
s: DRAGIN identifies LLM information needs across the full context by detecting tokens whose combined uncertainty, attention influence, and semantic score exceed a threshold, then uses their positions to trigger retrieval and truncate generated output.

l: DRAGIN, DRAGIN: Dynamic Retrieval Augmented Generation based on the Information Needs of Large Language Models
s: DRAGIN is a dynamic retrieval-augmented generation framework for large language models that makes retrieval decisions from their real-time information needs during text generation. Its central purpose is to address both when retrieval should occur and what should be retrieved, optimizing retrieval timing and query formulation without further training, fine-tuning, or prompt engineering for Transformer-based LLMs. During continual generation, Real-time Information Needs Detection (RIND) monitors generated-token importance and uncertainty to trigger timely retrieval. Query Formulation based on Self-attention (QFS) then uses the LLM’s attention over the entire context to formulate a precise query. DRAGIN retrieves external knowledge and continues generation using that knowledge. It is evaluated with three LLMs on four knowledge-intensive datasets covering multihop reasoning, reading comprehension, and commonsense reasoning. It achieves superior or strong results on all evaluated datasets, with especially substantial gains on 2WikiMultihopQA and HotpotQA; it outperforms FLARE, FL-RAG, and FS-RAG in its timing and query-formulation methods, while making fewer retrieval calls than FS-RAG and FL-RAG. Its threshold sensitivity is low across RIND settings, and its code, data, and models are open-sourced in the GitHub repository for DRAGIN.

l: experimental results, DRAGIN: Dynamic Retrieval Augmented Generation based on the Information Needs of Large Language Models
s: Experimental results from four datasets demonstrate DRAGIN's effectiveness, culminating in superior performance on all evaluated tasks.

l: large language models, DRAGIN: Dynamic Retrieval Augmented Generation based on the Information Needs of Large Language Models
s: Large language models generate text using Hugging Face code and may require external, real-time knowledge. Experiments use LLaMA-2-Chat-7B, LLaMA-2-Chat-13B, and Vicuna-13B-v1.5 with downloaded parameters and greedy decoding. Across benchmarks, retrieval augmentation helps most when DRAGIN activates it according to models’ information needs rather than fixed rules.

l: hallucination, DRAGIN: Dynamic Retrieval Augmented Generation based on the Information Needs of Large Language Models
s: is_a problem [commonly associated with large language model outputs] Hallucination refers to the production of text by large language models that appears coherent and plausible but is factually incorrect. Retrieval-Augmented Generation is presented as a prominent approach for mitigating this problem.

l: Retrieval-Augmented Generation, DRAGIN: Dynamic Retrieval Augmented Generation based on the Information Needs of Large Language Models
s: Retrieval-Augmented Generation is a retrieval-augmented strategy, solution, and framework that enhances large language models by retrieving relevant external knowledge from databases and incorporating it into model inputs. It is a prominent approach to mitigating hallucination and improving performance. Rather than relying only on traditional single-round retrieval from an initial input, it can support complex multi-step and long-form generation: output is truncated at a detected position, retrieved documents are added to a prompt, and generation resumes. Evaluations on 2WikiMultihopQA, HotpotQA, IIRC, and StrategyQA show improved performance over direct question answering, though poorly timed retrieval can be less helpful.

l: Real-time Information Needs Detection, DRAGIN: Dynamic Retrieval Augmented Generation based on the Information Needs of Large Language Models
s: Real-time Information Needs Detection is DRAGIN’s retrieval activation method and timing module, deciding when to retrieve during generation. It uses Transformer-based LLM self-attention and evaluates each generated token’s uncertainty, semantic contribution, and influence on following context. It quantifies uncertainty with entropy, influence with maximum following-token attention, and semantic significance through a binary stopword filter. Multiplying these factors yields a comprehensive token score; retrieval is activated when the score exceeds a predefined threshold. In DRAGIN, it provides timely activation. Threshold changes yield relatively stable HotpotQA performance, while higher thresholds reduce retrieval frequency and can trade efficiency against output accuracy.

l: Query Formulation based on Self-attention, DRAGIN: Dynamic Retrieval Augmented Generation based on the Information Needs of Large Language Models
s: Query Formulation based on Self-attention is DRAGIN’s proposed query formulation method for dynamic retrieval augmentation. At a position identified by Real-time Information Needs Detection, it examines the entire context through a Transformer-based LLM’s self-attention to determine information needs. It selects the top n preceding tokens by attention score, restores their original text order, and constructs a retrieval query from their corresponding words. It provides precise query formulation; experiments on HotpotQA show it outperforms the query methods used by FLARE, FL-RAG, FS-RAG, and full-context querying.

l: Transformer-based LLMs, DRAGIN: Dynamic Retrieval Augmented Generation based on the Information Needs of Large Language Models
s: Transformer-based LLMs provide the self-attention mechanism used for Real-time Information Needs Detection and Query Formulation based on Self-attention. The paper’s method depends on this mechanism.

l: self-attention, DRAGIN: Dynamic Retrieval Augmented Generation based on the Information Needs of Large Language Models
s: Self-attention is a Transformer-based LLM mechanism that allocates attention to tokens. It measures token influence to detect real-time information needs and formulate queries: following-token attention signals retrieval needs, while preceding-token attention identifies context for the next token; reliance on it is a primary limitation.

s: is_a off-the-shelf model [used to retrieve relevant information] The retrieval model uses the query produced by Query Formulation based on Self-attention to retrieve relevant information from external knowledge bases. An off-the-shelf model such as BM25 can serve this role.

s: Single-round retrieval augmentation uses the initial input to query an external corpus, then adds retrieved knowledge to model input; it can work well for simple needs but may lack sufficient knowledge for complex or lengthy tasks.

l: multi-round retrieval augmentation, DRAGIN: Dynamic Retrieval Augmented Generation based on the Information Needs of Large Language Models
s: is_suitable_for long-form question answering [complex tasks or tasks involving the generation of lengthy text] Multi-round retrieval augmentation retrieves information during generation and is explored for complex tasks such as long-form question answering, multi-hop reasoning, and chain-of-thought reasoning. RETRO and ICRALM trigger retrieval at fixed token intervals, IRCot triggers it every sentence, and FLARE triggers it when a generated token has a probability below a threshold.

s: External knowledge is retrieved from a corpus for input or generation in large language models, sometimes providing differing claims about Einstein’s 1903 job. It is also retrieved from knowledge bases as numbered references to support continuation after output truncation.

s: Multihop question answering is evaluated using 2WikiMultihopQA and HotpotQA, which require complex questions to be answered through multihop reasoning. Multihop reasoning is represented by 2WikiMultihopQA and HotpotQA in the evaluation. DRAGIN shows more substantial performance improvements on these tasks than on the common sense reasoning task StrategyQA.

s: FLARE is a dynamic RAG framework that triggers retrieval when next-token probability falls below a threshold. It forms queries from the last generated sentence, excluding uncertain tokens. Across datasets, it makes the fewest retrieval calls and is most efficient by that measure, though performance varies substantially by dataset and it remains below DRAGIN in reported timing and query-formulation comparisons.

s: BM25 is a lexical matching retrieval model and retriever. Adopted for strong retrieval-augmented generation performance, it outperforms some dense models and consistently surpasses SGPT across tested dynamic RAG datasets, concluding as a strong baseline for improving LLM RAG performance.

l: Wiki-LLaVA: Hierarchical Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Multimodal LLMs
s: The document presents Wiki-LLaVA, a retrieval-augmented multimodal large language model designed to answer visual questions and generate dialogues that depend on external knowledge. It begins by noting that LLMs and MLLMs perform strongly in zero-shot language and vision-language tasks but struggle with highly specific, compositional, and long-tail information not reliably stored in their parameters. Wiki-LLaVA addresses this limitation by augmenting LLaVA with retrieved text from an external multimodal knowledge source, such as Wikipedia, without substantially changing the underlying MLLM structure. The paper situates the method among LLMs, MLLMs, retrieval augmentation, and knowledge-based visual question answering. Its central mechanism is a hierarchical retrieval pipeline: CLIP-based image–title similarity first identifies relevant documents, then Contriever-based question-driven retrieval selects relevant passages. These passages are added to the model input alongside the visual and textual query. Training may fine-tune the system on knowledge-dependent question-answer pairs while mixing in examples that do not require external knowledge. Experiments evaluate Wiki-LLaVA on Encyclopedic-VQA and InfoSeek, studying Wikipedia retrieval, the contribution of retrieved context, and LLaVA-1.5 fine-tuning with dataset and LLaVA-Instruct samples. Results indicate that external knowledge substantially improves answers when the correct entity is retrieved, while incorrect retrieval can add harmful noise; oracle entities yield larger gains. The work also examines retention of general MLLM abilities. It concludes that hierarchical document and passage retrieval effectively augments MLLMs, while improved retrieval embeddings and document-selection methods remain key future directions. The work acknowledges CINECA, research grants involving Leonardo S.p.A. and Altilia s.r.l., FAIR, ITSERR, the European Commission, and NextGenerationEU.

l: Multimodal Large Language Models, Wiki-LLaVA: Hierarchical Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Multimodal LLMs
s: Multimodal Large Language Models are a vision-and-language model family and the natural evolution of LLMs beyond pure text. They combine visual-input understanding with natural-language generation, integrating visual features into LLM backbones through vision-to-language adapters. Using an image, textual prompt, visual context, and knowledge stored in parameters, they model a probability distribution and generate textual output autoregressively. They generalize well to elaborate visual descriptions, but may struggle with highly specific queries, compositional reasoning, and long-tail information. Methods developed different image-feature and language-model integrations; Wiki-LLaVA adds retrieved external knowledge to help answer questions requiring it.

l: Large Language Models, Wiki-LLaVA: Hierarchical Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Multimodal LLMs
s: Large Language Models are a model family and language models with remarkable language understanding and reasoning. They show impressive zero-shot textual performance, follow user-described tasks, and can be fine-tuned on varied natural-language tasks to assimilate instructions and generalize across domains. Instruction tuning and reinforcement learning from human feedback support alignment. They underpin multimodal systems: multimodal LLMs extend them beyond text, using visual tokens and optionally retrieved passages or external-memory tokens as context while generating text autoregressively.

l: answering questions that require external knowledge, Wiki-LLaVA: Hierarchical Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Multimodal LLMs
s: Answering questions that require external knowledge is the capability that the paper aims to provide to multimodal LLMs.

l: Wiki-LLaVA, Wiki-LLaVA: Hierarchical Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Multimodal LLMs
s: Wiki-LLaVA is a retrieval-augmented multimodal large language model and an approach for augmenting an existing MLLM, specifically LLaVA, with an external knowledge source of multimodal documents. It is designed to answer questions requiring external knowledge without significantly changing the MLLM’s structure. Its architecture comprises a visual encoder, a knowledge base, and a hierarchical retrieval module. The pipeline uses CLIP-based retrieval to identify relevant entities and Contriever-based passage retrieval to find textual chunks; selected document parts are then supplied as additional MLLM input context. Wiki-LLaVA uses Vicuna-7B as its language model and can be fine-tuned on Encyclopedic-VQA and InfoSeek, with LLaVA-Instruct as supplementary data. Extensive experiments evaluate it on visual-question-answering datasets with and without retrieved Wikipedia context, including settings using oracle entities. Results show improved effectiveness for questions and dialogues while maintaining proficiency across tasks; oracle retrieval improves performance substantially, and multiple textual chunks particularly benefit InfoSeek. Its main limitation is entity-retrieval quality, since irrelevant retrieved content can be passed to the MLLM.

l: external knowledge source, Wiki-LLaVA: Hierarchical Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Multimodal LLMs
s: The external knowledge source is a knowledge base of documents, including multimodal documents and Wikipedia as an example. Wiki-LLaVA accesses it through hierarchical retrieval, selecting relevant passages as additional context to augment an MLLM and improve answers. Its value is greatest when the correct entity is identified; incorrect entities can introduce noisy, uninformative context. In the no-knowledge setting, the MLLM instead relies only on learned competencies.

l: multimodal documents, Wiki-LLaVA: Hierarchical Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Multimodal LLMs
s: Documents are Wiki-LLaVA’s external knowledge and memory. They are retrieved by similarity between an input image and document titles, divided into chunks, and filtered for relevant passages that are included in the MLLM input context.

l: hierarchical retrieval, Wiki-LLaVA: Hierarchical Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Multimodal LLMs
s: The hierarchical retrieval pipeline gives Wiki-LLaVA access to an external knowledge source, supplying relevant passages as additional LLM context for questions needing precise external information. It first searches for entities using visual features, then retrieves textual chunks associated with selected entities, using approximate k-nearest-neighbor search through a Faiss HNSW index with 32 links per vertex.

l: passages, Wiki-LLaVA: Hierarchical Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Multimodal LLMs
s: Passages are retrieved from selected documents by similarity to a user's question and inserted as context to support LLMs and augment dialogues.

l: datasets tailored for visual question answering with external data, Wiki-LLaVA: Hierarchical Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Multimodal LLMs
s: supports visual question answering with external data The datasets tailored for visual question answering with external data are used in extensive experiments. The results demonstrate the appropriateness of the Wiki-LLaVA approach.

l: visual question answering with external data, Wiki-LLaVA: Hierarchical Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Multimodal LLMs
s: Visual question answering with external data is a task setting evaluated on Encyclopedic-VQA and InfoSeek, whose questions concern specific entities and often require external knowledge. The approach retrieves an entity and relevant passages, then supplies them to a multimodal large language model for answer generation. Accuracy is measured with official scripts; relevant retrieved context improves results, especially with two or three textual chunks on InfoSeek, while oracle retrieval performs substantially better.

l: hierarchical retrieval module, Wiki-LLaVA: Hierarchical Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Multimodal LLMs
s: The hierarchical retrieval module is an augmentation component for a multimodal large language model. It supplies appropriate external document knowledge, supporting diverse responses and assessment of retrieved content’s importance. It proceeds in two searches: image-to-title similarity selects documents, then the question selects passages within them.

l: InfoSeek, Wiki-LLaVA: Hierarchical Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Multimodal LLMs
s: InfoSeek is a dataset and benchmark for knowledge-based visual question answering and evaluating MLLMs with external data. It contains 1.3M image-question-answer triplets on about 11k entities, derives images from OVEN, uses Wikidata-filled templates, and evaluates retrieval on validation data.

l: Encyclopedic-VQA, Wiki-LLaVA: Hierarchical Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Multimodal LLMs
s: Encyclopedic-VQA is a benchmark dataset for evaluating MLLM capabilities with external data and knowledge-based visual question answering. It contains about 221k question-answer pairs for 16.7k fine-grained entities, over 1M image-question-answer triplets, and a 2M-article Wikipedia knowledge base. Training supports LLaVA fine-tuning; evaluation uses 4,750 filtered test triplets and finds CLIP retrieval difficult at this scale.

l: fine-tuning, Wiki-LLaVA: Hierarchical Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Multimodal LLMs
s: Fine-tuning is a classical approach that augments multimodal large language models by training on natural-language question–answer pairs requiring external knowledge, so models exploit retrieved passages. It uses low-rank adapters to reduce trainable parameters and is performed separately for two datasets with total batch size 512. It can degrade LLaVA-1.5 benchmarks; adding LLaVA-Instruct samples improves InfoSeek and better preserves benchmark performance.

l: external knowledge, Wiki-LLaVA: Hierarchical Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Multimodal LLMs
s: External knowledge is retrieved as textual input context to augment multimodal large language models. Because long-tail information is scarce in training data, it is difficult to encode internally. Retrieval supplies needed details for highly specific, external-knowledge questions, enabling more precise answers beyond image and pre-trained knowledge alone.

l: LLaVA, Wiki-LLaVA: Hierarchical Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Multimodal LLMs
s: LLaVA is a reference multimodal large language model. It introduces multimodal instruction tuning using a GPT-4-collected curated dataset, combining a pre-trained Vicuna large language model with a CLIP-based visual encoder through an MLP adapter. It extracts image features and prepends visual tokens to the system prompt.

l: retrieval augmentation, Wiki-LLaVA: Hierarchical Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Multimodal LLMs
s: Retrieval augmentation expands a model’s input with relevant external or web passages, improving knowledge-intensive tasks while reducing the need for larger models. Here, it augments multimodal large language models through hierarchical retrieval over a multimodal knowledge base.

l: Wikipedia, Wiki-LLaVA: Hierarchical Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Multimodal LLMs
s: Wikipedia is a large corpus and external knowledge base, supplied through two dumps and used to retrieve documents; its content is segmented into 600-character chunks and embedded with Contriever for retrieval.

l: CLIP, Wiki-LLaVA: Hierarchical Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Multimodal LLMs
s: CLIP is a pre-trained visual model used in a hierarchical retrieval pipeline. With the CLIP ViT-L/14@336 backbone, it encodes images and text to compute image–title similarity, retrieve target entities from query images, and provide LLaVA’s visual encoder. It retrieves more successfully from the 100k-entry InfoSeek knowledge base than the 2M-entry Encyclopedic-VQA knowledge base; errors can yield irrelevant passages.

l: Contriever, Wiki-LLaVA: Hierarchical Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Multimodal LLMs
s: Contriever embeds passages and retrieves relevant ones in Wiki-LLaVA’s hierarchical scheme, supplying them after or alongside image-based entity retrieval to support answer generation.

l: surfboard, Wiki-LLaVA: Hierarchical Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Multimodal LLMs
s: A surfboard is a narrow plank used in surfing, with history in Hawaii through Ochroma wood and association with the 1926 invention.

l: 1926 invention of the surfboard, Wiki-LLaVA: Hierarchical Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Multimodal LLMs
s: The example identifies 1926 as the answer to the question of when the sporting equipment was invented. The accompanying text states that the Ochroma wood surfboard's history originates in Hawaii in 1926.

l: CLIP ViT-L/14@336, Wiki-LLaVA: Hierarchical Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Multimodal LLMs
s: A visual encoder provides visual context to the MLLM, extracts a dense grid of input-image features in LLaVA, and queries an external knowledge base for retrieval.

l: external memory, Wiki-LLaVA: Hierarchical Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Multimodal LLMs
s: is_composed_of document [as a collection of document, image, and text-title triplets] The external memory consists of documents and provides the retrieval-knowledge tokens added to the MLLM input. Its contents are searched hierarchically for relevant documents and passages.

l: image, Wiki-LLaVA: Hierarchical Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Multimodal LLMs
s: The image supplies visual features to the MLLM and serves as the query for retrieving documents by comparison with document-title embeddings.

l: textual prompt, Wiki-LLaVA: Hierarchical Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Multimodal LLMs
s: The textual prompt usually contains a pre-defined system-level prompt and a question related to the input image. In the augmented method, it is combined with image tokens and retrieved raw chunks.

l: question, Wiki-LLaVA: Hierarchical Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Multimodal LLMs
s: The question is used both as part of the user prompt and as the query for retrieving relevant passages within selected documents.
